Lydda and Ramle

Massacre, Forced Expulsion, Death March · 1948-07-09 – 1948-07-13 · Operation Dani, 1948 Arab-Israeli War

1948-07-09 – 1948-07-13
Date
Lydda and Ramle
Location
≈400–1,000
Deaths
≈50,000–70,000
Displaced
Location, thenLydda (Al-Lydd) and Ramle (Al-Ramla), British Mandate of Palestine (under Israeli occupation from July 11-12, 1948)
Location, nowLod and Ramla, Central District, Israel; Cities renamed and repopulated; small Palestinian minority remains
PerpetratorsIDF Yiftach Brigade (11th Brigade); IDF 8th Armored Brigade; Operation Dani command structure
ClassificationWar Crime; Crimes Against Humanity; Ethnic Cleansing (Nakba)

Summary

On July 9–13, 1948, during Operation Dani under the command of Yigal Allon (with Yitzhak Rabin as deputy), Israeli forces captured Lydda and Ramle. In Lydda, city-wide shootings killed hundreds of civilians; the Dahmash Mosque massacre alone claimed 70–250+ lives (estimates vary). Moshe Dayan's 89th Battalion participated in ground operations.

Immediately after the takeover, expulsion orders were executed: the entire Palestinian populations of both towns—approximately 50,000–70,000 people, including refugees—were forced to march on foot toward Ramallah in extreme July heat. This 'death march' saw numerous deaths from thirst, heat exhaustion, and deprivation; survivors reported infants dying, people chewing grass for moisture, and soldiers preventing access to water.

Total deaths are estimated at 400–1,000 (including in-city killings and march fatalities). No perpetrators were prosecuted. Allon became Deputy Prime Minister; Rabin became Prime Minister and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1994); Dayan became Defense Minister and Foreign Minister. Rabin's memoir passages describing the expulsion order were censored in 1979, later restored.

Timeline

July 9–10, 1948
Operation Dani begins
Israeli forces advance toward Lydda-Ramle sector. Allon commands operation; Rabin deputy; Dayan leads ground battalion.
IPS/PalQuest
July 11, 1948
Assault on Lydda
8th Armored Brigade and infantry enter Lydda. Heavy fire reported; panic spreads. Ramle falls same day with less resistance.
IPS/PalQuest
July 12, 1948 (afternoon)
Dahmash Mosque massacre
Soldiers enter mosque compound; gunfire and grenades kill 70–250+ (estimates vary). Bodies piled inside and around mosque.
Munayyer memoir
July 12, 1948 (evening)
Expulsion order issued
Allon/Rabin command issues expulsion order. Rabin later wrote he asked Ben-Gurion 'What shall we do with the Arabs?' and received hand gesture to expel (censored from 1979 memoir).
Rabin memoirs analysis
July 12–13, 1948
Death march begins
50,000–70,000 Palestinians forced on foot toward Ramallah. Extreme heat (July); no water provided. Loudspeakers compel movement; soldiers prevent aid.
IPS/PalQuest
July 13–15, 1948
March continues; deaths mount
Infants, elderly die en route. Survivors describe chewing grass for moisture, bodies left along road. International observers later document suffering.
IPS/PalQuest

Testimony

Suleiman (Sami) Munayyer
“Describes fall of Lydda, city-wide panic, and Dahmash Mosque killings. 'Bodies piled inside the mosque. I helped burn corpses.' Estimates 70-80 killed at mosque; other accounts cite up to 250+.”
'The Fall of Lydda' memoir (archived PDF)
Reja-e Busailah
“Crowds were herded off the road into rough terrain. Loudspeakers compelled movement. The march brought exhaustion and death. Bodies left along the route.”
Memoir/testimony reproduced by IPS/PalQuest
Ismail Shammout
“People chewed grass for moisture. Infants died on the march. Attempts to obtain water were met with threats. I saw elderly collapse and die. The heat was unbearable.”
Interview excerpt cited by IPS/PalQuest
Yitzhak Rabin
“'What shall we do with the Arabs?' I asked [Ben-Gurion]. He waved his hand in a gesture meaning: Expel them. [This passage was censored from 1979 Hebrew edition of memoir; restored in later editions.]”
The Rabin Memoirs (1979/later editions); cited in Morris 2004

War crimes

City-Wide Shootings
Widespread killings in streets and homes during and after assault. Bodies reported throughout Lydda. Estimates: several hundred killed in city.
IPS/PalQuest Overview
Dahmash Mosque Massacre
Soldiers entered mosque compound where civilians sheltered. Gunfire and grenades killed 70–250+ (estimates vary widely). Munayyer describes bodies piled inside; he helped burn corpses. Among deadliest single incidents of 1948.
'The Fall of Lydda' (Munayyer memoir)
Forced Expulsion & 'Death March'
50,000–70,000 expelled on foot toward Ramallah in extreme July heat. Loudspeakers: 'Get out or we will shoot.' No water, no aid. Survivors: 'Crowds were herded into rough terrain... exhaustion and death.'
Survivor Testimonies
Deaths of Infants & Elderly on March
Ismail Shammout: 'Infants died on the march. People chewed grass for moisture. Attempts to obtain water were met with threats.' Elderly collapsed; bodies left along road.
IPS/PalQuest Testimonies
Denial of Water & Aid
Soldiers prevented access to water sources. Survivors report threats and violence when attempting to help collapsed marchers or seek water.
IPS/PalQuest Excerpts
Looting & Property Seizure
Homes looted during and after takeover. Property of expelled population seized. Lydda and Ramle renamed Lod and Ramla; repopulated with Jewish immigrants.
IPS Portal Entry

Legal classification

Law Applicable in July 1948
Hague Convention IV (1907): Customary by 1948. Art. 23(c): killing enemies who laid down arms; Art. 25: attack on undefended places; Art. 28: pillage; Art. 46: protection of family honor, lives, property; Art. 52: prohibition of collective punishments.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive Classification)
Geneva Convention IV (1949): Adopted Aug 12, 1949 (one month after Lydda). Israel ratified Jul 6, 1951; Jordan May 29, 1951. Art. 49: 'Individual or mass forcible transfers... are prohibited regardless of their motive.' Not applicable retroactively to July 1948.
Command Responsibility
Nuremberg Principles (1946): Established that commanders bear responsibility for crimes committed by subordinates if they knew or should have known and failed to prevent/punish.
Treaty Opposability
Vienna Convention principle: Treaties not retroactive (Art. 28). Geneva IV cannot be invoked for events predating its adoption.
Law Applicable in July 1948
Martens Clause (1899/1907): Humanitarian principles binding even where not explicitly codified.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive Classification)
Rome Statute (1998): Art. 7(1)(d): Deportation or forcible transfer (crimes against humanity); Art. 7(1)(a): Murder (CAH); Art. 8(2)(a)(i): Willful killing (war crimes); Art. 8(2)(b)(xxv): Intentionally starving civilians (war crime). Used descriptively; not retroactive enforcement.
Command Responsibility
Application to Operation Dani: Allon (operational commander), Rabin (deputy), Dayan (battalion commander), and Lahis (unit officer) held command positions during documented atrocities. Rabin's own memoir confirms knowledge at highest levels. No investigations or prosecutions pursued.
Treaty Opposability
Customary IHL: Hague 1907 + Martens Clause bound all parties in 1948 regardless of ratification.
Law Applicable in July 1948
Customary IHL: Prohibition of forcible transfer/deportation of civilians; obligation to allow access to essentials (water, medical care) during hostilities.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive Classification)
Note: Modern classifications aid understanding but do not create retroactive legal obligations.
Law Applicable in July 1948
Note: These instruments were opposable to all parties in 1948 as customary international humanitarian law.

Commanders

Yigal Allon
Operation Dani Commander (Palmach) — Overall operational command; authorized assault on Lydda-Ramle; issued or approved expulsion orders for both cities
Yitzhak Rabin
Deputy Commander, Operation Dani (Palmach) — Second-in-command; by his own account asked Ben-Gurion 'What shall we do with the Arabs?' and received hand gesture to expel. Directly involved in execution of expulsion orders.
Moshe Dayan
Battalion Commander, 89th Commando Battalion (Palmach) — Led ground assault on Lydda; commanded forces during city-wide operations and killings
Shmuel Lahis (Lahav)
Company Commander, 3rd Battalion, Yiftach Brigade — Directly implicated in Dahmash Mosque killings; led forces during house-to-house operations in Lydda
David Ben-Gurion
Prime Minister and Defense Minister — Ultimate political authority; according to Rabin's censored memoir, gave hand gesture to expel when asked about Arab population

Historical impact

Immediate Impact
Single largest expulsion event of 1948: ≈50,000–70,000 displaced from two cities in one operation
Long-term Significance
Central episode in Palestinian collective memory; 'Lydda death march' referenced alongside Deir Yassin
Accountability
✘ No perpetrators prosecuted for Lydda-Ramle killings or expulsions
Immediate Impact
Strategic gain for Israel: secured corridor to Jerusalem; captured what would become Ben Gurion Airport area
Long-term Significance
Historiographical controversy: Israeli 'New Historians' (Morris, Pappé) challenged official narratives in 1980s-2000s
Accountability
✘ Yigal Allon (commander) became Deputy PM & Foreign Minister; honored as Israeli hero
Immediate Impact
Humanitarian catastrophe: 'death march' became defining symbol of Nakba brutality
Long-term Significance
Rabin memoir censorship (1979) revealed in 1990s; became symbol of suppressed history
Accountability
✘ Yitzhak Rabin (deputy commander) became PM & Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1994)
Immediate Impact
Refugee crisis: expelled population strained resources in Ramallah/West Bank; many later fled to Jordan
Long-term Significance
Ongoing legal/political relevance: descendants of expelled cite Lydda-Ramle in right-of-return claims
Accountability
✘ Moshe Dayan (battalion commander) became Defense Minister & Foreign Minister; iconic military figure
Long-term Significance
Dahmash Mosque still stands in Lod; occasional site of commemorations despite restrictions
Accountability
✘ Shmuel Lahis (Dahmash Mosque) convicted 1950s for different incident; conviction overturned 2020; mosque killings never charged
Accountability
✘ Property never returned; Lydda/Ramle renamed Lod/Ramla; repopulated with Jewish immigrants
Accountability
✘ UN mediator Count Bernadotte (who documented expulsions) assassinated by Lehi September 1948
